country.paper_says: The study was conducted in São Gonçalo, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
country.where: p. 1, author affiliations and Abstract; pp. 2–3, Introduction

study_design.paper_says: “The methodological process, exploratory in nature and combining qualitative and quantitative approaches,” used in-situ household interviews with semi-structured questionnaires and descriptive socioeconomic and water-access data.
study_design.where: pp. 6–8, “Investigating another dimension of hydrosocial scarcity: verification method”

population.paper_says: Households were studied in one selected IBGE census tract in each of two neighborhoods, Mutondo and Jardim Catarina. The surveyed households represented 25% of the households in each tract—not 25% of census tracts.

sample_size.paper_says: The paper reports 45 households surveyed in Jardim Catarina and 46 in Mutondo, totaling 91 households.

urban_rural.paper_says: The research concerns urban water supply in two neighborhoods of São Gonçalo, in the Rio de Janeiro Metropolitan Region.

service_provider.paper_says: “Water abstraction and treatment are operated by the Rio de Janeiro State Water and Sewerage Company (CEDAE). Since 2021, distribution has been effected by the private company Águas do Rio.”
service_provider.where: p. 5, “Hydrosocial scarcity in São Gonçalo/RJ according to official data”

regulatory_model.paper_says: Federal Law 11,445/07 established universalization as a legal principle, and Law 14,026/20 set a 2033 universalization target. The paper separately attributes recognition of water and sanitation as a fundamental human right to the United Nations; it does not describe the two Brazilian laws themselves as establishing that human right.

effect_measure.paper_says: The study used an exploratory mixed qualitative-quantitative design, typical-case sampling, semi-structured household questionnaires, and descriptive comparisons between neighborhoods. It does not report a socioeconomic-indicator correlation analysis or a formal effect measure.

effect_estimate.paper_says: The study found that connection to the public system did not guarantee reliable access: poorer Jardim Catarina experienced intermittent, weak-pressure and insufficient supply, whereas better-off Mutondo generally had daily, uninterrupted supply. The authors characterize this as hydrosocial scarcity invisible in official connection statistics and a failure to realize effective universal access.
effect_estimate.where: pp. 14–18, “Discussing the second dimension of hydrosocial scarcity” and Final remarks

extraction_note.paper_says: The paper contains no internal review record identifier against which “RF20B9AADA984” can be verified.

parsed.overall_comment: Several substantive findings are captured correctly, especially the urban Brazilian setting and invisible scarcity among formally connected low-income households. However, the design, sampling description, sample size, provider structure, legal characterization, and claimed correlation require correction.
